passage: After Disha, five, grabbed another child's pencil case, Mehak Ma'am sat down beside her. "I'll be good, I promise, I promise," said Disha, eyes wide. "I believe you want to," said Mehak. "It's hard to remember when we're excited. What could help you remember?" Disha thought. "A star." They drew a star on a card and stuck it on her desk. "When you feel like grabbing, look at the star, and ask."

qa.q: What did Disha and Mehak put on Disha's desk?
qa.a: A card with a star drawn on it.

qa.q: What was Disha feeling when she said "I promise"?
qa.a: Sincere regret and a wish to be good. She may also have hoped to avoid more trouble.

qa.q: How did Mehak treat the promise?
qa.a: As a hope, helping Disha plan how to keep it with a star reminder and a way to ask.

qa.q: How might the child whose pencil case was grabbed feel about the promise?
qa.a: Perhaps still upset until the pencil case is back. The promise alone does not fix it, and what Disha does next matters more.

grounding: Shows a preschooler promising to be good with sincere intent and a teacher helping her plan to keep it.

passage: I'm Parveen from the ground floor. Every evening Ujjwal, five, shouts in the stairwell, "I'll be good tomorrow, I promise!" On Tuesday his ball landed in my plant pot and he said, "I'll never do it again!" The next day it happened again, and he stood there sheepish. His father said, "How about playing on the far side of the yard?" "I promise to play at the far side," said Ujjwal, and together they moved the goal. He seems to mean it each time.

qa.q: What did Ujjwal promise after his ball landed in the plant pot?
qa.a: That he would never do it again.

qa.q: Did Ujjwal mean his promise, and what suggests it?
qa.a: Probably sincerely, since he stood there sheepish afterwards, but he seems not yet able to keep it. Parveen can only guess.

qa.q: How did Ujjwal's father help him keep his promise?
qa.a: He suggested a plan, playing on the far side of the yard, and moved the goal there with Ujjwal.

qa.q: How might Parveen feel about the ball landing in her plant pot?
qa.a: Somewhat annoyed but patient, since she seems to treat it as a child's slip.

grounding: Shows a child promising to be good with sincere intent but limited ability, with his father turning the promise into a plan, seen by a neighbour.

passage:
Sunday night: Ishita promised Wasim, her father, “Tomorrow at the toy shop I will be good. I won't ask for anything.” She meant it.
Monday, in the shop: She saw a sparkly unicorn and begged for it, then cried when he said no.
Wednesday: Wasim didn't say, “You broke your promise.” He said, “Your promise was a hope. Let's make a plan.” Ishita chose: she would hold the shopping list and tick things off.
Saturday: In the shop, Ishita held the list tight and ticked the boxes. She looked at the unicorn once, then said, “Not today.”

qa.q: What did Ishita see in the shop on Monday?
qa.a: A sparkly unicorn.

qa.q: What was Ishita feeling when she promised to be good on Monday?
qa.a: She was sincere and hopeful; she truly meant it but did not yet know how hard it would be.

qa.q: What did Wasim do that helped her keep her promise?
qa.a: He treated the promise as a hope and made a plan with her, giving her the list to hold and tick.

qa.q: What would change if Wasim had said “You broke your promise”?
qa.a: Ishita might feel ashamed and learn that promises lead to blame, rather than learning how to keep them.

grounding: Over a week, a preschooler's sincere promise to be good fails, and her father treats it as a hope and helps her plan how to keep it.

passage: The relatives were arriving in twenty minutes, the house was a mess, and Salma was frying pakoras. Kunal hugged her leg. “I promise I won't fight with Zoya today.” Salma knew he meant it and knew Zoya always took his cars. She turned down the flame for one minute and knelt. “I love that promise. What will you do when she takes your car?” Kunal thought. “Say ‘My turn next’?” “And if she doesn't give it?” “Come to you.” “Good plan.” She went back to the pakoras.

qa.q: What did Kunal promise?
qa.a: That he wouldn't fight with Zoya today.

qa.q: What was Kunal feeling when he hugged his mother's leg and promised?
qa.a: He felt sincere and hopeful, wanting to please her, but a little unsure how the day would go.

qa.q: Which choice by Salma worked, and why?
qa.a: She took a minute to help him plan what to do when Zoya took his car, turning his promise into steps he could follow.

qa.q: How might Zoya experience the day if Kunal uses his plan?
qa.a: She'd likely get a calm “My turn next” instead of a fight, making play easier for both.

grounding: Under time pressure, a mother treats her preschooler's promise as a hope and helps him plan how to keep it.

passage: In the city school, before assembly, Neelam whispered to Aparna Ma'am, “I promise I won't talk today.” Yesterday she had chatted all through the prayer. Aparna smiled; she knew Neelam meant it and knew how hard it was. “Thank you. What will help you?” Neelam shrugged. “Maybe stand near you?” “Good idea. And if you want to talk, squeeze your hands together.” During assembly, Neelam squeezed her hands three times and whispered only once. Afterwards Aparna gave her a thumbs-up.

qa.q: How many times did Neelam squeeze her hands during assembly?
qa.a: Three times.

qa.q: What was Neelam feeling when she whispered her promise?
qa.a: She felt sincere and hopeful, perhaps a little worried about keeping it after chatting the day before.

qa.q: What did Aparna Ma'am do that helped Neelam keep the promise?
qa.a: She thanked her and helped her plan: stand near the teacher and squeeze her hands when she wanted to talk.

qa.q: How might Aparna Ma'am see Neelam's one whisper?
qa.a: She sees it as real progress, not a broken promise, which is why she gives a thumbs-up.

grounding: A teacher treats a preschooler's promise as a hope and helps her plan how to keep it during assembly.

passage:
"Mumma, I promise I'll be good at the wedding. Really, really good."

Uma smiled. "That's a lovely hope, Sangeeta. It's a long evening, though. What might be hard?"

Sangeeta thought. "Sitting still. And the loud drums."

"So what can we do when that happens?"

"I can squeeze your hand when I'm bored?"

"Good plan. And if the drums are too loud?"

"We go outside for a bit."

"Deal. And if you forget, that's okay. We'll just try again."

Sangeeta held out her little finger. "Pinky promise."

Uma linked hers. "Pinky plan."

qa.q: What did Sangeeta say might be hard at the wedding?
qa.a: Sitting still, and the loud drums.

qa.q: What was Sangeeta feeling when she promised to be "really, really good"?
qa.a: She was most likely sincere and hopeful, wanting to please her mother. Naming the hard parts suggests she was also a little worried about the long evening.

qa.q: How did Uma turn the promise into something Sangeeta could keep?
qa.a: She treated it as a hope, asked what might be hard, and helped Sangeeta plan what to do, such as squeezing her hand or going outside.

qa.q: How does Uma feel about the promise?
qa.a: She is warm and pleased, but realistic, so she tells Sangeeta that forgetting is okay and they can try again.

grounding: It shows a preschooler making a sincere promise to be good and an adult treating it as a hope and helping her plan how to keep it.
